name: Speedb
workload: Massive random-write workload: database with 80 million objects, 1KB values, 50 threads, measuring sustained write throughput and stalling over time.
claimed_speedup: Sustains consistent write throughput without the write-stalls RocksDB exhibits under the same load, via a new delayed-write mechanism (graph only, no numeric ops/sec ratio stated)
tradeoffs: 100% RocksDB API-compatible drop-in; Speedb Ltd (the company) reportedly wound down in 2024, matching the last-commit date.
caveats: README shows only a chart, no exact throughput numbers, CPU model, or compiler flags; docs.speedb.io (which may have more detail) was unreachable this session (TLS connection failed).

name: count-db
workload: JNI-bound Java benchmark writing/reading 1M-256M Wikipedia bigram counts (8 threads), plus a uniform-random-count test, against LevelDB, RocksDB and Kyoto Cabinet.
claimed_speedup: Up to ~80x faster than LevelDB writing 256M bigram counts and ~11x faster reading; also faster than RocksDB and Kyoto Cabinet in the same tables (e.g. uniform-count write: count-db 1.48E7 vs LevelDB 1.56E5, RocksDB 1.07E5 ops/sec)
hardware: Intel i7-4770, SATA 6Gb/s 7200rpm HDD, 32GB RAM (10GB JVM heap)
tradeoffs: Optimized narrowly for primitive counters/counts and simple serialized objects; no SQL-style querying or transactions.
caveats: Old (2015-era) spinning-disk hardware, no SSD; JVM version/flags unstated; first-party benchmark; the largest ratio (~80x) exceeds the >50x implausibility threshold, which is why this is capped at tier C rather than higher despite detailed tables.

name: Pogreb
workload: Random point-lookup read benchmark of pogreb vs goleveldb (LevelDB Go port), bbolt and badgerdb, using the separate pogreb-bench tool.
claimed_speedup: Higher random-read throughput than goleveldb, bbolt and badgerdb in the read-heavy benchmark chart (no exact numeric ratio given in text, chart image only)
hardware: DigitalOcean droplet, 8 CPUs, 16GB RAM, 160GB SSD, Ubuntu 16.04.3
tradeoffs: Hash-table index makes range scans impossible; single hash table shared across WAL segments means recovery requires rebuilding the entire index (slow at large scale).
caveats: pogreb-bench is a separate repo but written by the same author as pogreb, so first-party; no exact numbers in README text, only a linked chart image; Go version/build flags not stated.

name: HaloDB
workload: 500 million records, 8-byte keys / 1024-byte values (~500GB, IO-bound): fill-sequential, random-read (32 threads, 640M reads), random-update, fill-random, and mixed read+update tests, vs RocksDB and KyotoCabinet.
claimed_speedup: Charts show higher throughput than RocksDB and KyotoCabinet across fill/read/update tests; author states no exact numeric ops/sec figures are given in the doc, only graphs
hardware: 2x Xeon E5-2680 2.50GHz (24 cores/48 threads HT), 128GB RAM, 1x Samsung PM863 960GB SSD (XFS), RHEL 6, kernel 2.6.32
tradeoffs: No range scans or ordered access; entire key set + metadata must fit in memory; startup requires scanning all keys to rebuild the in-memory index.
caveats: Author explicitly states HaloDB is not always better than RocksDB and only a subset of RocksDB's features are supported, so comparison 'is not exactly fair to RocksDB'; JVM version/flags unstated; first-party benchmark.

name: SurrealKV
workload: 50,000 keys, 48 concurrent worker threads, 128 clients, synchronous durability (--sync) via the crud-bench cross-engine harness; point read, create, update, delete and scan operations.
claimed_speedup: 3.31x faster creates, 3.08x faster updates, 2.84x faster deletes, 2.31x faster point reads, 3.47x faster range scans vs RocksDB (also beats Fjall, SlateDB; LMDB/Libmdbx win on some ops, e.g. LMDB scan)
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper 9970X (32-core/64-thread) @5.48GHz, 128GB DDR5 RAM, 4TB PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD, bare metal
tradeoffs: Higher resting memory than RocksDB (~328MB vs ~356MB is comparable, but peak differs); versioned/MVCC design trades some write-path complexity for read/write concurrency.
caveats: crud-bench is maintained by the same org (SurrealDB) as SurrealKV, so despite covering many engines it is not fully independent; Rust compiler version/release flags are not stated on the page.

name: Starskey
workload: 10,000 ops with 32-byte keys/values: write, get, delete benchmark against Pebble, BBolt, Badger, LMDB and RocksDB, single-threaded, via the starskey-io/bench tool.
claimed_speedup: Write ~53ms and delete ~29ms per 10k ops vs RocksDB's ~287ms and ~283ms (roughly 5-9x); but LMDB is faster than Starskey on every operation in the same table (e.g. LMDB write 3.7ms)
hardware: Unspecified — author describes it only as a "crappy 4 year old system"; no CPU model given
tradeoffs: LevelDB-WiscKey inspired LSM design; small single-run benchmark, no repeated trials or variance reported.
caveats: Hardware and Go build flags are unstated; the benchmark's own numbers show LMDB (this category's other named baseline) beating Starskey on every metric, so the 'faster than incumbents' claim only holds narrowly against RocksDB.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "faster than LevelDB" --sort stars --limit 30

name: TidesDB (seek/range-query benchmark vs RocksDB)
workload: 5 million point-seek operations, 8 concurrent threads, 16-byte keys / 100-byte values, sync disabled, TidesDB v6.1.0 vs RocksDB v10.7.5.
claimed_speedup: 4.17x faster random seeks (3.73M vs 893K ops/sec, 2us vs 8us median latency), 4.74x faster sequential seeks, 5.25x faster Zipfian-distributed seeks; range-query performance described as "competitive but not dominant" versus RocksDB
hardware: Intel Core i7-11700K (8 cores/16 threads) @4.9GHz, 48GB DDR4, Western Digital Blue 3D NAND 500GB SATA SSD, Ubuntu 23.04 x86_64, kernel 6.2.0-39-generic
tradeoffs: Aggressively keeps SSTable metadata (block indices, bloom filters, min/max keys, file handles) resident in memory to eliminate disk I/O on the seek path, trading memory footprint for latency; CPU utilization is higher than RocksDB in the same test (469% vs 635%—note TidesDB is actually lower here).
caveats: TidesDB itself is already catalogued (KNOWN_LIST); this entry records a new, higher-quality Tier A benchmark for it discovered via its own blog (surfaced through Hacker News), separate from its repo README. Raw benchmark report and benchtool source are linked from the article. The author's own "Honest Assessment" section notes range queries are not a clear win.
found_via: HN Algolia: query="faster than RocksDB" tags=story -> https://tidesdb.com/articles/benchmark-design-range-seek-tidesdb610-rocksdb1075

name: AnuDB
workload: Raspberry Pi: JSON-document insert/query/update/delete and parallel-operations benchmark (10,000/1,000/5,000/2,500 ops respectively) via the AnuDBBenchmark repo, AnuDB (RocksDB-backed) vs SQLite3.
claimed_speedup: ~2.34x higher ops/sec than SQLite3 in the parallel-operations test (AnuDB processed 4x more operations, 10 threads vs SQLite3's 4); AnuDB is also ~1.23x faster on queries, but SQLite3 is 3.9x faster on inserts, 2.1x faster on updates, and 5.3x faster on deletes in the same table
tradeoffs: AnuDB is a JSON-document layer built on top of RocksDB (not a from-scratch storage engine); embedded-only, no client/server mode besides an optional MQTT interface.
caveats: The project's Show HN title claimed "279x Faster Than SQLite in Parallel Workloads," but that figure does not appear on the linked benchmark page/repo, whose own table shows only a ~2.34x parallel advantage with unequal thread/op counts between engines, and SQLite winning most other categories outright. Reported here using only the number that is actually on the page, per the hard rule against inventing numbers.
found_via: HN Algolia: query="embedded key-value store" tags=story -> "Show HN: AnuDB– Backed on RocksDB, 279x Faster Than SQLite in Parallel Workloads", cross-checked against https://github.com/hash-anu/AnuDBBenchmark

name: ZoneTree
workload: Live profile-store workload, 2,000,000 profiles: individual inserts, primary-key reads, secondary-index (email) lookups, ordered index scans, indexed range queries, updates, and post-update re-reads, with deterministic checksums verifying identical result sets across engines.
claimed_speedup: Total run time 181s (ZoneTree) vs 429s (RocksDB, ~2.4x faster, derived from page data) vs 1,062s (SQLite, ~5.9x faster, derived from page data); lookup-by-email 388,867/s (ZoneTree) vs 138,471/s (RocksDB) vs 277,620/s (SQLite); RocksDB's raw insert throughput (154,360/s) is slightly ahead of ZoneTree's (141,281/s) including stabilization
hardware: AMD EPYC 4345P 8-Core Processor (16 logical processors), 60.4GB available memory, Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS, X64
tradeoffs: Uses substantially more peak process memory than RocksDB in this benchmark (3.3GB vs 1.1GB) in exchange for higher read/query throughput; ZoneTree and RocksDB secondary indexes are maintained by the benchmark application (separate stores) while SQLite/MySQL maintain them natively, so the storage layouts differ even though results are checksum-identical.
caveats: Multiple reference sizes (100K-100M profiles) are published; numbers above are from the 2M-profile report specifically. Benchmark is a single custom workload (profile store), not a general-purpose comparison, and the project explicitly warns against generalizing.

name: lsm-tree-go
workload: Linux, 4 CPU, 1 million keys, 11-byte keys+values, batch size 1000: sequential write, random write, read, and miss-read throughput vs BoltDB and BadgerDB.
claimed_speedup: 5x faster than BoltDB on random writes (1.19M ops/sec vs 0.23M ops/sec); still ~4x behind BadgerDB, which lsm-tree-go does not beat
tradeoffs: Small personal/teaching LSM-tree implementation, not a hardened production engine; read throughput (0.44M/s) is lower than both BoltDB and BadgerDB in the same table.
caveats: No LICENSE file in the repo, so code is 'reference' only (study/reimplement, don't copy); CPU model and Go toolchain version are not stated; BoltDB, the beaten baseline, is not one of this category's named incumbents (RocksDB/LevelDB/LMDB/SQLite) though it is a widely used embedded KV store.
